paragraphs.text:
The teacher of the Church is like a physician. The Church suffers from many different ailments, and he gives each of the sick the remedy their ailment requires. For instance, some came into the Church's surgery suffering from the swelling disease of pride; they received the plaster of humility and were healed of that swelling. Others ran to it inflamed with anger; they too were soothed by the [?] of the soul, and their sickness was quenched. Still others came running, driven to lust by the passions of the flesh; they too received the plaster of self-control and bound themselves up in chastity. Come then, beloved: since the teacher who spoke before me treated the souls of the sick with the threefold faith, let us also follow in his footsteps. I think, too, that many of those standing here want to hear about the faith, not because they need it themselves, for they are healthy, but because they want to use it to heal the sick. For many people are healthy themselves but are unable to heal those who are unwell. So, beloved, although I meant to break open the text of the Gospel that was just read to you, and to give those present the Spirit itself to drink, I am putting that off and doing what I promised instead. For since we are disciples of the apostle, we must become all things to all people, so that we may win them all. I ask you, too, to forgive us if we stumble over our words. Those who speak without preparation often stumble, since the mind is not equal to studying Scripture and adorning the speech at the same time. And you yourselves, present the inner man of your heart here as pure as you can, so that each of you may not only hear what is said but also see it, and learn the force of each thing.

First, then, faith toward God is something incomprehensible, intangible, invisible, beyond accusation, honoured and worshipped in silence. Faith begins from the Father, comes to the Son, and is completed in the Spirit. Faith is the seat of the soul, the foundation of life, an undying root; and the living root of faith is the Father, its unfading branch the Son, its undying fruit the Holy Spirit. The Trinity is simple, uncompounded, inexpressible, indescribable, undivided in harmony, in power, in operation, in Godhead, in greatness; distinguished in hypostases and names, united in its works and powers. The Trinity exists before the ages. It did not begin to be from some beginning, but is without beginning, timeless, ageless, immortal, without end; it does not grow or diminish, it does not age, but is indestructible. It remains the same Trinity. It was not discovered just now as an object of worship; from all ages it has been worshipped by angels in heaven, glorified by the fathers on earth, honoured by the prophets, proclaimed by the apostles, and magnified by the Church to this day.

Let us begin, beloved, from the heavens; let us begin to show the one lordship, worship and majesty of the Trinity. Three times the highest angels and powers, the Cherubim and Seraphim, singing "Holy, holy, holy" with unceasing voice, bring their glory to its summit in one lordship. When the patriarch Abraham, beneath the oak of Mamre, saw three angels at his tent, he gave the trinity of angels one lordship, an equality. The three angels, the oak, the tent and Abraham: [?] the cross, the Church and the offspring of humankind. Abraham himself went a three days' journey to offer his son Isaac to God as a whole burnt offering. The three days' journey and Isaac offered as a burnt offering: the three-day passion of the Only-begotten through the cross. That Abraham saw the mystery of Christ in Isaac, the Lord testifies when he says, "Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day; he saw it and was glad." Moses too goes a three days' journey to sacrifice to God. So he says to Pharaoh, "We will go a three days' journey to sacrifice to the Lord our God." Sarah also took three measures of fine flour and made cakes baked in the ashes. The three measures of fine flour, Sarah and the hidden cakes: the threefold faith and the Church, kept in the hidden place of the human heart. Jacob took three rods, put them in the water and watered Laban's sheep. Three rods, water, and sheep being watered: the Trinity, baptism, and a people being enlightened. Jonah spent three days and three nights in the whale. The three days and nights, Jonah and the whale: [the three days] of the Only-begotten in Hades. And that this is so, let him say himself: "Just as Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so must the Son of Man spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth." The Ninevites too fasted for three days and lived. Three days, fasting, and the Ninevites living: the light-bearing Trinity, abstinence from evil, and the life of the world. Three times the prophet Elijah poured water on the split wood and the pieces of the bull, and brought fire down on them from heaven. The threefold water, the split wood, the pieces of the bull and the heavenly fire: the threefold baptism, the cross, the members of Christ and the heavenly light. Daniel too, opening the windows of his house toward the east three times a day and praying, obtained his request, the mystery teaching us that we must open the eyes of the soul and pray toward the east to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Three undefiled youths were thrown into the furnace of fire; they suffered nothing themselves, but burned up the Chaldeans. The three undefiled youths, the furnace and the Chaldeans: the incorruptible Trinity, the judgment, and the demons perishing. The blessed Paul hands on three virtues to the Church, saying, "Faith, hope, love": faith in the Father, hope in the Son, and love, the fulfilment of the law; for the fruit of the Spirit is love. Paul himself also entreated the Lord three times, saying, "Three times I entreated the Lord about this." And notice the man's wisdom packed into the simplest of words. He did not say, "I entreated the Lord a third time," but "three times": Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three hypostases but one lordship. "And three times," he says, "I was beaten with rods"; that is, I confessed three hypostases, but once for all, with the stone of confession, I set my soul firm in the faith of the Trinity, in one harmony. "And three times," he says, "I was shipwrecked"; that is, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit I sank the cargo of Jewish sins in the font of baptism. The kingdom of heaven too was likened to three measures of flour, which a woman took, and hid a little leaven in it, and leavened the whole lump. The three measures of flour, the little leaven and the woman leavening it are Wisdom, which through the body of Christ turns all humanity to faith in the Trinity.

Setting a kind of seal on all these mysteries, our Lord handed on to his disciples one baptism in three immersions of the body, saying, "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." We shall readily show that there is one operation; and once one operation of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is shown, it necessarily follows that one essence must also be believed, for those whose operation is one have also one essence. Let us begin, then, to speak of the making of the world, of adoption, of freedom, of the founding of heaven and earth, and, in a word, of every work and of the provisions for the other needs of our life, all accomplished by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Let us begin from the first things, go on to the second, and so bring our discourse safely through in order.

The Father made heaven, but not without the Word and the Spirit: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the Spirit of his mouth." The Father filled the whole world, as it is written: "I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord." The Son also filled it: "For all things came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being." Hear Wisdom speaking about the Spirit: "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world." What more? The greatest of created things, man, was not brought into being by the Father alone, but with the Son working together with him and the Holy Spirit completing the work. For he says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." "Let us make": not "I will make," nor "you will make," nor "he will make," but "let us make." Had he said, "You make him," he would have been pointing to a subordinate; but to teach their equal honour he says, "Let us make man." The counsel is shared, the act is shared, and the creature is shared. That Father, Son and Holy Spirit made man, David testifies to me when he says to God, "Your hands made me and formed me." You did not make me alone; your hand alone, which is your Only-begotten, did not make me. "Your hands made me," that is, the Word and the Spirit. It is as though he said: the wisdom of the Word formed me, the understanding of the Spirit made me, with you completing the work. Likewise Job says to God, "Your hands formed me and made me." For the heavens and the host of the heavens came into being through him, as David says: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the Spirit of his mouth"; and in the prophet Hosea: "Whose hands created the host of heaven." For here too he indicates that the host of the heavens was created through the Spirit and the Word.

"Let us make man in our image": not "in our images," but "let us make man in our image." "Let us make" is plural, but "in our image" is singular. And so that no one would suppose that man came into being in the image of the Father alone, he added "our." And for this reason, since that first-formed image of Adam, estranged by the transgression, needed renewal and cleansing, it is renewed in baptism not in the name of the Father alone, but also of the Son and the Holy Spirit, since that is how it came into being from the beginning. Certainly the Father seals in baptism, as Paul says: "He who prepared us for this very thing is God, who anointed us and sealed us." And the Holy Spirit also seals: "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption." When our hearts are sealed by the Father and the Spirit, we are not transformed into two images, but into one, that of his Son. From this it follows that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one. When our hearts are sealed, we become conformed to the Son and the image of God, as Paul cries out: "A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God." How much more, then, is the Holy Spirit the image of God!

The Son is great, and the Holy Spirit is boundless. "Great is our Lord, and great is his power" (for Christ is the power of God), "and of his understanding there is no number"; that is, the Holy Spirit of God is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding. The Father is peace: "Behold, I will turn toward them like a river of peace." The Son too is peace, as Paul says: "He is our peace, who has made both one." The Holy Spirit too is peace: "The fruit of the Spirit," he says, "is love, peace." The Father is a fountain: "For with you is the fountain of life." The Son too is a fountain: "For they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." And if the Holy Spirit were not also a fountain, Paul would not have said, "And we were all baptized in the one Spirit." But we can learn more fully from the Lord's own words that the Holy Spirit is likened to a fountain. For Jesus came and cried out, saying, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink water; and, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly." He said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive. The Father is light, for "God is light"; the Son too is light, for "I am the light of the world"; the Spirit too is light, otherwise Paul would not have said, "Do not quench the Spirit." But since some find this forced, let David state it explicitly: "In your light we shall see light," that is, the Holy Spirit. The Father sets free the one enslaved to sin; the Son sets free, for he said to the Jews, "If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed"; the Spirit too sets free, for "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." The law of the Spirit sets free: "The law of the Spirit has set you free from the slavery of corruption." The Father is good, and the Son is good: "Is your eye evil," he says, "because I am good?" The Holy Spirit too is good: "Your good Spirit will lead me on level ground." The Father is wherever he wills, for he has no one to whom he is subject; the Son too is wherever he wills, for he is free; the Spirit too is wherever he wills: "The Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes." The Father contains all things, the Son contains all things, and the Holy Spirit contains all things; for David says, "Where shall I go from your Spirit? And where shall I flee from your presence?" The Father is almighty, as Job says: "I know, Lord, that you can do all things, and nothing is impossible for you." The Son is almighty, as he says in the Gospel to the man who was slow to believe: "All things," he says, "are possible to the one who believes." The Holy Spirit too is almighty. For this power of God, it says, is the Holy Spirit, "a spirit intelligent, holy, manifold, subtle, mobile, clear, distinct, unharmed, keen, unhindered, beneficent, loving humankind, steadfast, sure, free from care, almighty and overseeing all." And the Holy Spirit not only oversees all, but also makes human beings overseers, as Paul testifies to me in the Acts, saying, "Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers."

The Father sent prophets, the Son sent prophets, and the Holy Spirit also sent them, as one of the prophets, Isaiah, declares: "And now the Lord, the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." The apostles were sent out by the Son: "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves." They were also sent out by the Holy Spirit, as it says in the Acts: "So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia." The Father called the apostles, the Son called the apostles, and likewise the Holy Spirit called them: "While they were ministering to the Lord" (who? the apostles), "the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them.'" "You set them apart; set apart for me Barnabas and Paul. I speak as master; obey as servants." "While they were fasting and ministering to the Lord." Pay attention: "and ministering." Where are those who say the Holy Spirit is a ministering spirit? If the Holy Spirit is a ministering spirit, he is one of the angels and of the holy apostles; for "he makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire." But the Holy Spirit is not one who ministers but one who is ministered to: "While they were ministering," it says, "the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me.'" That is the voice of a master: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them." "Now you set apart for me Paul and Barnabas; for I have already set them apart from their mother's womb." And since Paul was called by the Holy Spirit, and set apart by the apostles for the gospel, as he says in his first epistle: "A servant, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God."

But now, beloved, those who are at leisure for blasphemy, when they ought to be at leisure for the divine Scripture and to know the Lord and the saying, "Be at leisure and know that I am God," have found something new. Now they have found another blasphemous question, and they question us, saying, "Does the Father have a throne?" And we say, "Yes: for God sits on his holy throne." "Does the Son also have a throne?" We say, "Yes," for it is written of the Son: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever." But when you hear of God's throne, you must understand the throne in a way fitting to God, that is, as authority, kingship, lordship; for Scripture speaks to us as to human beings. "Then where is it written," they say, "that the Holy Spirit also has a throne, so that, recognizing his equal honour from the throne, we may ascribe lordship to him?" Strictly, we ought not even to answer such people when they ask such a question. For if servants made from earth, I mean the apostles, were counted worthy to sit on thrones ("Behold, you twelve will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel"), how much more the Holy Spirit! On top of this they ask, "Where is the Spirit's glory? The Father is glorified, the Son is glorified; where is the Holy Spirit?" So the unbelievers inquire. Let the faithful answer, and let Isaiah bear witness: "I saw the Lord on a throne, high" (he is speaking of the Spirit, as will shortly be shown) "and lifted up, and the house was full of his glory. And Seraphim stood around him; six wings to the one, and six wings to the other; and they cried out, 'Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts; heaven and earth are full of your glory.'" Pay attention here, and look at both the throne and the glory. "And the Lord said to me, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people,'" of the Jews? "And he will say to them, 'Hearing you will hear and will not understand; for the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard heavily,'" and so on. Paul comes many years after the prophecy. He is in Rome, he reasons with the Jews, trying to persuade them into faith in the Only-begotten; but they turned away and refused to believe. Then he recalls this prophecy, because it had been fulfilled. And what does he say to them? "Well did the Holy Spirit speak about you through Isaiah the prophet: 'Hearing you will hear and will not understand,'" and so on. See: the one whom Isaiah calls the Lord of hosts, seated on a high throne and glorified by angels, Paul says is the Holy Spirit. Who is still so mad as to doubt that the Spirit is both Lord and God and worthy of worship? To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
